BCCC Post Hearing Initial Brief             2         June 19, 2026
 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

       Burnet County Commissioners Court (“BCCC”) submits this Post-Hearing Initial Brief in

the Joint Application of Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC. (“Oncor”) and LCRA

Transmission Service Corporation (“LCRA”) to Amend Their Certificates of Convenience and

Necessity for The Bell County East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-Kv Transmission Line

Project In Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell, Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam,

Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green, and Williamson Counties (“Joint Application”).

       First, BCCC would like to thank the Administrative Law Judges (“ALJs”) for their

incredible work in this case. Cases in the CREZ proceedings that were close to this size had a trial

schedule of two weeks. To no fault of the ALJs, the very reduced time for cross-examination of

the witnesses, although needed to complete the trial in the short one-week schedule, was not

sufficient to fully vet the issues in this case. BCCC would also like to commend the pro se

intervenors for their preparation and commitment to the case. They performed amazingly well in

the hearing. Finally, Joint Applicants are to be commended. They had multiple CCNs processing

at the same time that this hearing took place. It is not surprising that things were missed under this

tight schedule. As was discussed in the Commission’s Open Meeting on Wednesday, June 17,

2026, changes to this process are very needed.

       I.      INTRODUCTION

       BCCC continues to believe the routes offered by the Joint Applicants do not conform to

PURA 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC 25.101. Furthermore, the data provided by Joint Applicants in

their environmental assessment (“EA”) is incorrect and stale. By providing incorrect and stale

data, Joint Applicants shifted the burden to the landowners to prove the correct data at the hearing.




BCCC Post Hearing Initial Brief                   3                                    June 19, 2026
 Not only was the information in the EA stale, but so is the ERCOT Study under which the entire

Permian Basin Plan is based.

       Finally, BCCC requests that if any route is granted (all of which traverse Burnet County),

that SOAH and the Commission add ordering paragraphs to require the Joint Applicants to: 1)

commission an independent study to learn how to avoid interference with emergency management

communication systems; and 2) to work with BCCC to ensure that the placement of the towers

along the route do not interfere with BCCC’s emergency management communication systems.

       II.       JURISDICTION AND DEADLINE FOR DECISION
       BCCC believes that the Commission has jurisdiction over this docket under PURA and the

Commission’s rules. BCCC disagrees with the Joint Applicants in asserting the 180 days under

PURA 37.057 is a jurisdictional deadline. The Commission does not lose jurisdiction after 180

days if no decision is made. The 180 days is a statutory deadline with an included remedy: the

applicants may seek a writ of mandamus requesting that the Commission issue an order in the

docket.1     The CCN is not automatically granted nor denied, and the Commission retains

jurisdiction until a final decision is made.


       III.      PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES

       A.        JOINT APPLICATION

              1. Is the joint applicants’ application to amend their CCN adequate? Does the
                 joint application contain an adequate number of reasonably differentiated
                 alternative routes to conduct a proper evaluation?

       No. The Joint Application did not contain an adequate number of reasonably differentiated

alternative routes to conduct a proper evaluation. Instead, Joint Applicants forced a narrow study



       1
           PURA 37.057.



BCCC Post Hearing Initial Brief                 4                                  June 19, 2026
 area stating that the Fort Hood military base and the cities around it prevented them from

considering more northern routes along compatible rights of way.2 Joint Applicants also stated

that other constraints prevented them from considering more southern routes.3 Sadly, Joint

Applicants did not even consider routes outside of Burnet County.4 In fact, Joint Applicants

refused to consider any analysis along compatible rights of way offered by BCCC.5 The Joint

Applicants instead made conclusory statements about the area north of Burnet County without any

analysis that the ALJs and Commission could consider.6 In an answer to a BCCC RFI inquiring

whether the Applicants ever considered using Interstate 190 when leaving the Bell Station, they

answered:

       Utilizing a corridor parallel to, or in the vicinity of US 190 upon leaving the Bell

       East Substation was never considered as a viable option because of the amount of

       development and structures along either side of US 190 as it goes through Temple,

       Belton, Harker Heights, and Killeen. Aside from these construction constraints,

       routing along Interstate 190 would also require federal approval from the Fort Hood

       military base.7

There is no evidence in the record of the constraints along Interstate 190 and beyond, nor

any evidence that Fort Hood refused to allow any transmission lines around its property.

        B.          NOTICE

       2. Did the joint applicants provide notice of the application in accordance with 16
          TAC §22.52(a)(1), (2), and (3)?

       No. The Texas Administrative Code requires that “[t]he applicant must, on the date it files

an application, mail notice of its application to the owners of land, as stated on the current county

tax rolls, who would be directly affected by the requested certificate.”8 Throughout the hearing

intervenors questioned the Joint Applicants regarding why their habitable structures were not

included and why they did not receive notice. The Joint Applicants first testified that they used

the county tax records that were current when they mailed notice.9 The testimony was clearly

rebutted at length by at least one intervenor.10 The Joint Applicants then testified that they

“[s]erved·notice to all the landowners per the current tax --·county tax roll at the time that [they]

pulled the data, sir.”11·Joint Applicants pulled data from between December 2024 and March 26,

2026.12 The date for the tracts reflected in the interactive map was from May 2025 to February

2026.13 The limited afore-cited testimony, reflects that at least twenty-seven (27) landowners were

not provided notice.14 During the hearing, others provided information that clearly showed the data

was stale.15

       D.         NEED

       5. Taking into account the factors set out in the Public Utility Regulatory Act
          (PURA) § 37.056(c), are the proposed transmission facilities necessary for the
          service, accommodation, convenience or safety of the public within the meaning
          of PURA § 37.056(a)? In addition, please address the following issues:
              a. How do the proposed transmission facilities support the reliability and
                 adequacy of the interconnected transmission system?
              b. Do the proposed transmission facilities facilitate robust wholesale
                 competition?
              c. What recommendation, if any, has an independent organization, as defined
                 in PURA § 39.151, made regarding the proposed transmission facilities?
              d. Are the proposed transmission facilities needed to interconnect a new
                 transmission service customer?

       6. In considering the need for additional service under PURA § 37.056(c)(2) for a
          reliability transmission project, please address the historical load, forecasted load
          growth, and additional load currently seeking interconnection.

       7. Are the proposed transmission facilities the better option to meet this need when
          compared to using distribution facilities? If the joint applicants are not subject to

               the unbundling requirements of PURA § 39.051, are the proposed transmission
              facilities the better option to meet the need when compared to a combination of
              distribution facilities, distributed generation, and energy efficiency.


        The question of need is very much a contested issue in this docket. In fact, legislators have

continued to engage with the Commission and within the docket to seek a reconsideration of

whether all of these 765kV lines are really needed.18 When cross-examining the Joint Applicant

panel, Mr. Martin admitted that a letter from ERCOT in December 2024 stated that only two of

the three import paths were needed by 2030.19

        In their Joint Application, Joint Applicants stated that part of the original need for the

project for the non-oil and gas loads was the expected cryptocurrency centers (59%), data centers

(6%), green hydrogen (22%) and commercial/industrial consumers (13%) that were estimated to

be built.20 Of that load, only 39% was confirmed by actual contracts.21 Interestingly, in December

2024, the Regional Transmission Plan was revised to lower the estimated crypto load to 18% and

increase the data center load to 46%.22 By the time of the 2025 Regional Transmission Plan was

filed, the non-crypto data center load was estimated to be 55% of the total growth, followed by

hydrogen/ammonia planning at 16%, industrial and manufacturing load at 13%, crypto load at 9%

and oil and gas load at only 7%.23 The report did not identify expected growths without the oil

and gas load, as they had previously provided. What are the results now? Are the underlying

 assumptions still that data center growth will continue? The December 2024 and December 2025

Regional Transmission Plans were included in the rebuttal testimony of the Joint Applicants, as

cited. Because of the short timeline and number of parties involved, Joint Applicants required on

a ten-business day discovery deadline. Any discovery on rebuttal would not be due until after the

hearing started. With only thirteen (13) minutes to cross-examine the panel, further information

could not be gleaned. BCCC’s focus had to be on protecting its emergency communication

systems.

        Recently many citizens of Texas have voiced opposition to data centers. The Governor of

Texas even instructed the Commission to pass rules requiring data centers pay for their actual share

of these new transmission lines and not allow residential consumers to subsidize this cost.24 If data

centers are required to absorb their costs caused by their interconnection, they may choose to co-

locate generation, use behind the meter generation, enter into power purchase agreements or not

build in Texas.

        Generic constraints in the Permian Basin could be solved by building oil and gas generation

behind the constraints to offset the problems for incoming generation. Of course, the negative

prices in that area due to renewable energy is a disincentive for dispatchable generation to invest

in building new generation. The Commission has tried for decades to encourage independent

power producers to build new generation in ERCOT. A competitive market is not supported by

overbuilding transmission. The market needs to be a balance of transmission and dispatchable

generation. It is time to reconsider the market design in the ERCOT market. The steps taken thus

far have not yielded the results the market needs. Spending billions of dollars on transmission that

will change the landscape of Texas forever, while placing a scar on Texas land and the burden of


        24

BCCC Post Hearing Initial Brief                        9                                       June 19, 2026
 the cost on residential ratepayers, is not the answer. It will still not attract new dispatchable

generation.

       BCCC requests that the Commission place a pause on this process while it reconsiders a

holistic solution to this problem.

       E.         ROUTE

       8. Weighing the factors set forth in PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B),
          which proposed transmission line route is the best alternative?

       BCCC is against ALL routes going through Burnet County. Furthermore, the routing data

in the environmental assessment, in total, are incorrect and stale.25 The EA is relied upon by all of

the parties when arguing their positions before, during and after the hearing.                             When that

information is not correct, it compromises the entire process. The Joint Applicants propose that if

the data is not correct, the burden is then on the landowner to correct it and place the burden on

the ALJs to revise the EA to allow them to make decisions based upon real facts rather than faulty

data. Of course, only the intervenors who were allowed to remain the in the case could provide

such evidence. When an intervenor is provided only 13 minutes, as in this hearing, to cross

examine the Joint Applicants’ entire panel, this process is prejudicial and highly burdensome.

Rather than having confidence in the information the Joint Applicants provide through their EA,

instead the ALJs and Commission must comb through all of the cited evidence to determine the

correct information, and then hopefully make the correct determination after this grueling exercise.

The burden should remain on the Joint Applicants throughout the process to provide correct data.

As it is seen from the evidence in this proceeding, the Joint Applicants failed to do so, which is

another basis to deny this CCN application.

         a.          Statutory criteria
               i.   Community Values
                    PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)

              ii.   Recreational and park areas
                    PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(B)

             iii.   Aesthetic and historical values
                    PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(c)

             iv.    Environmental Integrity
                    PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D)

        The Commission has interpreted “community values” as a “shared appreciation of an area

or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community.26 Parks and

recreational areas are measured only within 1000 feet from the transmission line in the EA rather

than the actual visual impact from the park or recreational area. The Joint Applicants’ EA includes

only historic areas that have been registered with the various state agencies at the time they request

the information. Regarding environmental integrity, the EA includes only “apparent property

boundaries” rather than actual property boundaries, a standard not included in the rule.27

        This 765kV line will have far more impact than any other transmission line ever built in

Texas. As Judge Wilson states in his testimony addressing all of these issues:

        ONCOR and LCRA has set two linked segments of the proposed lines along and

        across three critical riparian streams, the Lampasas River, the North Fork of the San

        Gabriel River, and the Middle Fork (Russell) of the San Gabriel River. On the

        western portion of Burnet County, the lines pass along or across Deer Creek,

        Morgan Creek, Silver Creek, Spring Creek, Lacy Creek, Beaver Creek, Wolf Creek

       endangered mollusk and at least two protected avian species. These streams form

       the foundation of the drainage into the Colorado and Brazos Rivers and are major

       recharge zones to sustain human and wildlife in the northern portion of the county.

       In Burnet County, surface water and ground water are intricately linked and

       interdependent. The denuding of the riparian basins will cause irrevocable and

       permanent destruction. This undermines the preservation of the dedicated funding

       purposes. ONCOR and LCRA deliberately chose these streams beds even though

       the PURA directs the avoidance of these types of environmentally sensitive

       routes.28

        ONCOR and LCRA failed to study or consider the implication of the 765kV lines

       on the impact to the historic legacy and ongoing productivity of the ranches and

       small businesses covering the northern Burnet County. The designation of Heritage

       Ranches by the Texas Department of Agriculture has been state policy and practice

       since the 1970s. The total disregard of the historic significance is contrary to the

       state and local efforts by the Texas Historical Commission, the Burnet County

       Historical Commission, and the Texas Department of Agriculture. The proposed

       lines fail to address the impacts of these lines on calving, forage production, apiary

       production and general health of the land that makes a significant portion of the

       $2.7 billion economy.29

                                                 ....

       The 765kV Transmission line proposed routes will cause irreversible destruction of

       Indian burial mounds and innumerable prehistoric campground. Burnet County was

       home to Comanche, Apache, and many other tribes. I am aware of dozens of

       landowners reporting pre-historic findings along the proposed routes in Burnet

       County. The Burnet County Historical Commission has been working with

       landowners to document these and other findings. The installation of the massive

       towers and the construction easement clearing will erase prehistoric sites from

       existence.30

       The routes through Burnet County undermine the preservation of the dedicated funding

purposed for State Parks and Rivers, destroys the scenic character and productively of large,

 generational ranches, and assaults the sensitive environmental areas including historical cultural

artifacts, wildlife habitat and other undisturbed rights of way. This could be resolved by following

already-disturbed rights of way such as highways, roadways, railroad tracks and other transmission

lines.

               v. Probable improvement of service of costs to consumers
                  PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(E)

         Although Joint Applicants in its Joint Application assert that building these 765kV lines

will ultimately save consumers money, just this portion of the Permian Basin project is between

$1.64 and $1.86 billion dollars.31 There is no record evidence that this CCN will improve service

or reduce costs to the consumers in this Burnet County.

         b. Commission rule criteria
            i. Engineering Constraints
               16 Tax § 25.101(b)(3)(B)
         BCCC’s three witnesses all testified to their concerns regarding the potential of the

transmission towers and lines to interfere with their emergency public safety communications

systems.32 Judge Wilson, who is the Chief Executive of the Western Regional Radio System (a

component of the Statewide Interoperability Communication System), the Burnet County

Emergency Management Director under Chapter 418 of the Texas Government Code, the primary

coordinator of public health under various statutes in the Texas Health and Safety Code and the

Judge of the County Court, noted that Burnet County has four towers in the study area.33

        Commissioner Beierle testified that “during wildfires, severe weather events, medical

emergencies and disaster response operations, reliable communications are essential.”34

Commissioner Luther testified that Burnet County has had emergency service communication

issues along its northern border. And that the County has invested significant effort and money to

address the problem.35 Burnet County erected several communication towers across the northern

portion of the county to ensure communication with emergency providers is not interrupted.36

Commissioner Beierle requested that the Commissioner require independent technical analysis

demonstrating that the proposed CCN will not negatively affect these systems.37

       Upon cross examination of the Joint Applicants’ panel of witnesses, none seemed to have

experience or knowledge with how transmission towers and lines can interfere with emergency

public safety communication infrastructure. They did not know where the BCCC towers were

located.38 The Manager, Transmission Design Engineer for LCRA, Mr. Elliott, reviewed research

published by EPRI, the Saturday night before the hearing.39 Mr. Elliott did not cite to the research.

Mr. Elliott did not know the frequency of the Greater Austin/Travis Regional Radio System

(“GATTRS”) of which Burnet County participates, but knew it was in the megahertz band.40 Mr.

Elliott responded with the same answer for VHF, UHF, and microwave systems.41 Mr. Elliott

testified that he believed that none of the transmission lines would interfere with any the

               i. Moderation of impact on the affected community and landowners

                    16 TAC §25.101(b)(3)(B).
        BCCC incorporates the previous portions of this brief into this section.


              ii. Paralleling
                  16 TAC §25.101(b)(3)(B)(i-iii) criteria

        To determine the best-meets route for a proposed transmission line, the Public Utility

Commission of Texas must consider: "(i) whether the routes parallel or utilize existing compatible

rights-of-way for electric facilities, including the use of vacant positions on existing multiple

circuit transmission lines; (ii) whether the routes parallel or utilize other existing compatible rights-

of way, including roads, highways, railroads, or telephone utility rights-of way; (iii) whether the

routes parallel property lines or other natural or cultural features; and (iv) whether the routes

conform with the policy of prudent avoidance.51

        The ALJs and Commission cannot accurately evaluate this issue without considering areas

north of Burnet County, information that the Joint Applicants refused to provide.

             iii.    Prudent Avoidance
                     16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv)

        The Commission’s policy on prudent avoidance instructs utilities to limit the exposures so

electric and magnetic fields that can be avoided with reasonable investments of money and effort.52

        52

BCCC Post Hearing Initial Brief                     17                                   June 19, 2026
 BCCC urges the Commission to add reasonable investments of money and effort to accomplish

this requirement.

          c. Best Route Alternative


       BCCC will not address this issue except to say that there is NO best route alternative that

can be found in this CCN.

                                  IV.     CONCLUSION
       BCCC respectfully requests that the ALJs and the Commission reject the Joint Application

for the reasons set forth in this brief. BCCC also supports other elected officials requesting an

updated study and consideration of market design before any transmission lines are approved. In

the alternative, if a route is approved in this docket, BCCC requests that the ALJ’s and

Commissioner add ordering paragraphs that the Joint Applicants be required to 1) commission an

independent study to learn how to avoid interference with emergency management communication

systems before any transmission lines are built; and 2) to work with BCCC to ensure that the

placement of the towers along the route do not interfere with BCCC’s emergency management

communication systems.

       First, BCCC would like to thank the Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs") for their

incredible work in this case. Cases in the CREZ proceedings that were close to this size had a trial

schedule of two weeks. To no fault of the ALJs, the very reduced time for cross-examination of

the witnesses, although needed to complete the trial in the short one-week schedule, was not

sufficient to fully vet the issues in this case . BCCC would also like to commend the pro se

intervenors for their preparation and commitment to the case. They performed amazingly well in

the hearing. Finally, Joint Applicants are to be commended. They had multiple CCNs processing

tight schedule. As was discussed in the Commission' s Open Meeting on Wednesday, June 17,

2026, changes to this process are very needed.

       I.      INTRODUCTION

       BCCC continues to believe the routes offered by the Joint Applicants do not conform to

PURA 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC 25.101. Furthermore, the data provided by Joint Applicants in

their environmental assessment ("EX') is incorrect and stale. By providing incorrect and stale

data, Joint Applicants shifted the burden to the landowners to prove the correct data at the hearing.

        II.       JURISDICTION AND DEADLINE FOR DECISION

        BCCC believes that the Commission has jurisdiction over this docket under PURA and the

Commission's rules. BCCC disagrees with the Joint Applicants in asserting the 180 days under

PURA 37.057 is a jurisdictional deadline. The Commission does not lose jurisdiction after 180

days if no decision is made . The 180 days is a statutory deadline with an included remedy : the

applicants may seek a writ of mandamus requesting that the Commission issue an order in the

docket.1      The CCN is not automatically granted nor denied, and the Commission retains

jurisdiction until a final decision is made.

         The Commission has interpreted "community values" as a "shared appreciation of an area

or other natural or human resource by a national, regional, or local community.26 Parks and

recreational areas are measured only within 1000 feet from the transmission line in the EA rather

than the actual visual impact from the park or recreational area. The Joint Applicants' EA includes

only historic areas that have been registered with the various state agencies at the time they request

the information. Regarding environmental integrity, the EA includes only "apparent property

boundaries" rather than actual property boundaries, a standard not included in the rule.27

                                   IV.    CONCLUSION
       BCCC respectfully requests that the ALJs and the Commission reject the Joint Application

for the reasons set forth in this brief. BCCC also supports other elected officials requesting an

updated study and consideration of market design before any transmission lines are approved. In

the alternative, if a route is approved in this docket, BCCC requests that the ALJ's and

independent study to learn how to avoid interference with emergency management communication

systems before any transmission lines are built; and 2) to work with BCCC to ensure that the
